6300:
Flip means to turn something over quickly with a sharp, light motion. Think of the action — fast, clean, often with a flick of the wrist. A pancake flips when it spins in the air and lands on its other side. A coin flips when you toss it so it rotates before landing. This sudden, complete turning motion is the soul of the word.

Everything else the word means is built on this same idea: a quick, complete change of some kind.

1. To turn something over quickly

The most basic, physical meaning. You flip an object when you rotate or turn it over with speed.

  • "Flip the pancake before it burns."
  • "He flipped the card over to see what was on the back."
  • "Flip the mattress — it'll be more comfortable."

The key detail: flipping is always quick. You don't slowly rotate something — you flip it in one sharp motion.

2. To toss something casually and lightly

When you flip something to someone, you throw it in a relaxed, effortless way — usually a short distance, usually without much force. It suggests ease and casualness.

  • "She flipped the keys to her brother across the room."
  • "The shopkeeper flipped the change onto the counter."
  • "He flipped a coin to decide who would go first."

Flipping a coin specifically means launching it into the air with your thumb so it spins, and then seeing which side faces up when it lands. This is a classic way to make random decisions.

3. To move a switch or lever sharply

You flip a switch, lever, or latch when you move it quickly from one position to another — off to on, closed to open, and so on.

  • "Flip the light switch when you leave."
  • "She flipped the safety switch before starting the machine."
  • "Just flip that lever and the water will start."

One quick motion, and the state of something changes completely.

4. To browse through something quickly

When you flip through a book, magazine, notebook, or TV channels, you move through them rapidly without reading or watching everything carefully. You're scanning, getting a general feel — not studying.

  • "He flipped through the magazine in the waiting room."
  • "She was flipping through channels trying to find something to watch."
  • "I flipped through the report to get the main idea."

You can flip through anything that has pages, sections, or options — physical or digital.

5. To suddenly lose emotional control

When someone flips (or flips out), they suddenly and dramatically lose their temper or composure. They have an extreme reaction — usually anger, but sometimes panic or wild excitement. The suddenness mirrors the physical flip.

  • "My dad is going to flip when he sees this."
  • "She flipped out when the airline lost her bag."
  • "Don't tell him yet — he'll flip."

This is very common in casual spoken English. When someone "flips," their emotional state has turned completely in an instant.

6. To completely change sides or switch allegiance

When someone flips in a situation involving loyalty or position, they turn completely from one side to the other — like a coin landing on its opposite face.

In legal and criminal settings, a criminal who "flips" agrees to cooperate with the police or prosecutors, often testifying against former partners in exchange for a lighter punishment.

  • "The suspect flipped and gave the investigators the names of everyone involved."
  • "The prosecutor spent weeks trying to convince him to flip."

In politics or public opinion, a person flips when they reverse their stated position on an issue — especially if they once held the opposite view.

  • "The senator flipped on the immigration bill after the election."
  • "He used to support the policy, but he's flipped completely."

In both cases, someone who was on "one side" is now on the "other side."

7. To buy something cheap and sell it quickly for profit

This is one of the most common modern uses of the word. When you flip something, you buy it at a low price — often something undervalued, damaged, or unpopular — improve it or wait for the right moment, and then sell it at a higher price for a profit.

Real estate is the most famous example:

  • "They buy rundown houses, renovate them, and flip them for profit."
  • "House flipping became very popular as a way to make money."

But the same idea applies to almost anything:

  • "He flipped old sneakers — buy limited editions cheap, sell them when the price rises."
  • "She flipped used books online."
  • "Traders sometimes flip stocks within hours."

The word captures the speed and the reversal: something goes from low-value to high-value and then changes hands quickly.

8. To perform an acrobatic rotation

In gymnastics, diving, or informal physical activity, to flip means to throw your body through a complete rotation in the air — like a somersault.

  • "The gymnast flipped across the mat and landed perfectly."
  • "He flipped off the diving board into the pool."
  • "She's been learning how to do a back flip."

The body literally "turns over" in mid-air — same core motion, applied to the whole body.

9. A vehicle rolling over

When a car, truck, or boat flips, it rolls over completely — usually in an accident.

  • "The car skidded on the ice and flipped onto its side."
  • "The boat flipped in the storm and everyone had to swim to shore."

Flip through — to browse quickly and lightly
"Flip through the chapter before the lecture."

Flip out — to suddenly lose composure; to go crazy with anger, panic, or excitement
"She flipped out when she found out she'd won."

Flip over — to turn something completely to its other side; or (of a vehicle/object) to roll over
"Flip the steak over now." / "The canoe flipped over in the rapids."

Flip off — (informal, rude) to make a rude gesture at someone by raising the middle finger at them; it's considered very offensive
"The driver flipped off the car that cut him off."

Flip the script — (idiom) to reverse a situation entirely; to turn the tables so that what was working against you now works in your favor
"She was being pressured at the negotiation, but she flipped the script and put them on the defensive instead."

In British English especially, "flipping" (and sometimes "flip") is used as a mild, socially acceptable substitute for a stronger swear word — expressing frustration or surprise without being offensive.

  • "What the flip is going on here?"
  • "That's absolutely flipping ridiculous."

It softens the emotion while still expressing it clearly.

Every single meaning of "flip" shares the same DNA: something changes quickly and completely — a pancake turns over, a switch changes state, a criminal switches sides, a house changes ownership at a profit, a person's emotions go from calm to explosive. The motion is always fast, often decisive, and usually complete.

Once you feel this core — a quick, complete reversal or change — every use of "flip" will make sense naturally, even in sentences you've never seen before.
6301: "Flip off" has two distinct meanings in English. The first is far more common and culturally significant. The second is more literal and straightforward. You need to know both, because context determines which one is meant.
Meaning 1: To Make a Rude Gesture at Someone (Primary Meaning)

This is the most important meaning, and the one you will encounter most often.

When someone flips another person off, they raise their hand and extend only the middle finger (the longest finger) upward while keeping all other fingers curled down. This gesture is deeply offensive and carries a meaning roughly equivalent to saying a very strong, vulgar insult — something along the lines of "I hate you," "Go to hell," or a very rude dismissal.

Why is it called "flipping off"?

The word flip here refers to the quick, sharp motion of snapping or flicking the finger upward. The off suggests directing that gesture away from yourself and at the other person — as if throwing contempt in their direction. So, "flipping someone off" = turning your middle finger sharply toward them.

What emotion does it express?

It expresses a range of strong negative feelings, including:

  • Anger — "You made me furious."
  • Contempt — "I have zero respect for you."
  • Defiance — "I refuse to follow your rules. You can't control me."
  • Dismissal — "I don't care about you at all."

It is never a friendly gesture. Even if someone does it jokingly between very close friends, it is still understood as mock-aggression.

Grammar: How is it used in a sentence?

"Flip off" is a transitive phrasal verb in this meaning, which means it almost always takes an object — the person the gesture is directed at.

Structure: Subject + flip(s)/flipped + off + Object
Or: Subject + flip(s)/flipped + Object + off

Both word orders are acceptable:

  • She flipped off the rude driver.
  • She flipped the rude driver off.

If you use a pronoun (him, her, them, me, us) as the object, the pronoun must go in the middle, between "flip" and "off":

✅ He flipped her off.
❌ He flipped off her. — This sounds unnatural with a pronoun.

Real-life example sentences

  • The cyclist was so angry that he flipped off the car that almost hit him.
  • The teenager got in trouble at school for flipping off her teacher.
  • I can't believe he flipped me off just because I honked my horn!
  • She quietly flipped him off under the table so no one else could see.

Register and Tone

This expression is informal, vulgar, and offensive. You should:

  • Never use it in formal settings — job interviews, business meetings, academic writing, or in front of authority figures.
  • Be careful using it even casually, because it describes a highly offensive act.
  • Use it descriptively (talking about the gesture) rather than as a command directed at someone.

Cultural note

This gesture and phrase are especially common in American English, though it is also widely understood in other English-speaking countries. In some cultures, the equivalent gesture uses different fingers, but the middle-finger meaning of "flip off" is a distinctly North American English expression rooted in American slang.

Related expressions with the same meaning

All of the following refer to the same middle-finger gesture:

  • Give someone the finger — "She gave him the finger."
  • Flip someone the bird — "He flipped them the bird."
  • Give someone the middle finger — more literal and descriptive.
  • Shoot someone the bird — less common, but used in some American regions.
Meaning 2: To Turn Something Off (Secondary Meaning)

This meaning is much more literal. "Flip off" can simply mean to switch something off using a quick flipping motion — usually referring to a light switch, a power switch, or any toggle switch.

The word flip here describes the physical motion of pushing a switch downward or in the "off" direction. Think of a light switch on a wall — you flip it up to turn the light on, and flip it down (or off) to turn the light off.

Example sentences

  • Don't forget to flip off the lights when you leave the room.
  • She flipped off the switch as she walked out.
  • Can you flip off the TV? I'm trying to sleep.

How common is this meaning?

This usage is less common than Meaning 1. Most people simply say "turn off," "switch off," or "flick off" in everyday conversation. You might hear Meaning 2 mainly in casual American spoken English, particularly in certain regions.

Grammar note

Just like Meaning 1, this is also a transitive phrasal verb. The object is the thing being switched off (the lights, the TV, the radio, etc.).

  • He flipped off the generator. ✅
  • He flipped the generator off. ✅
  • He flipped it off. ✅ (pronoun goes in the middle)
How to Tell the Two Meanings Apart

Context makes it almost always obvious:

  • If the sentence is about a person being "flipped off," it is Meaning 1 (the rude gesture). You cannot flip off a lamp at a person.
  • If the sentence is about a machine, switch, or device being "flipped off," it is Meaning 2 (turning it off). You don't give a middle finger to a light bulb.

Compare:

  • "He flipped off his boss." → Rude gesture. He made an obscene middle-finger gesture at his boss.
  • "He flipped off the machine." → He turned the machine off.

Meaning 1Meaning 2
What it meansTo make a rude middle-finger gesture at someoneTo switch/turn something off
Object typeA personA device or switch
RegisterVulgar, informalCasual, informal
How commonVery commonLess common

Because Meaning 1 is so dominant and so strongly associated with this phrase, if you ever use "flip off" in conversation, people will most likely assume you're talking about the rude gesture — unless it's very clear from context that you're talking about a switch. To be safe and avoid misunderstanding, when you mean Meaning 2, it's better to just say "turn off" or "switch off."
6302:
"Flip out" is an informal American English idiom. It has two closely related meanings, and the context usually makes it clear which one is being used.

Meaning 1 (Most Common): To suddenly lose control of your emotions — especially out of anger, shock, or extreme stress.

Think of it this way: imagine a switch inside a person's brain. Normally, the switch is in the calm, controlled position. When something pushes that person too far, the switch "flips" — and they explode emotionally. That sudden loss of emotional control is what "flip out" captures.

"My dad flipped out when he saw the dent in his car."
(= He got extremely angry and probably shouted, panicked, or reacted very strongly.)

Meaning 2 (Less Common but real): To become wildly excited or thrilled about something.

In this sense, the emotion is positive — joy or excitement — but the intensity is the same. The person's emotions go out of their normal, calm range, just in a happy direction this time.

"She completely flipped out when she found out she won the lottery."
(= She became overwhelmed with excitement and joy.)

The key idea in both meanings is the same: a person's emotions suddenly shoot beyond the normal, controlled range — whether it's rage or joy.

To understand idioms better, it always helps to look at the individual words:

  • Flip — In everyday English, "flip" means to turn something over suddenly and sharply. Think of flipping a coin or flipping a pancake — it's a fast, uncontrolled turning motion.
  • Out — Here, "out" suggests going beyond limits, escaping, or losing containment. Think of "bursting out," "breaking out," or "losing it."

So "flip out" gives a mental image of something inside a person snapping and going beyond control — which is exactly what the idiom means.
Where Did This Idiom Come From?

"Flip out" is rooted in mid-20th-century American slang, particularly from the 1950s–1960s. It is closely related to older idioms like:

  • "Flip your lid" — Your "lid" is slang for the top of your head (like a lid on a pot). If the lid flips off, the steam escapes violently — a perfect image for losing your temper.
  • "Flip your wig" — Same idea. A wig flying off your head suggests sudden, uncontrolled chaos.

Over time, these phrases were shortened and simplified to just "flip out," which became the standard form we use today.

"Flip out" is a phrasal verb (a verb + a particle that together create a new meaning). It follows standard phrasal verb grammar.

You can use it in different tenses:

TenseExample
Simple Present"He always flips out under pressure."
Simple Past"She flipped out at the meeting."
Present Perfect"I've never flipped out like that before."
Progressive"He was flipping out over the exam results."

Note: "Flip out" cannot be separated. You cannot say "He flipped his emotions out." The two words always stay together.

Here are examples across different situations so you can see how natural speakers use this idiom:

Anger / Stress:

  • "The teacher flipped out when the students wouldn't stop talking."
  • "Don't tell Mom about the broken vase — she'll flip out."
  • "He completely flipped out when the airline lost his luggage."

Excitement / Joy:

  • "The kids are going to flip out when they see their Christmas presents."
  • "She flipped out when her favorite band announced a reunion tour."
  • "I flipped out when I got into my dream university."

Nervousness / Panic (less common, but used):

  • "I was flipping out before my job interview — my hands were shaking."

"Flip out" describes a strong, visible reaction — not just mild annoyance or quiet happiness. There is always a sense that the person's emotions have escaped their control, even briefly.

Think of it on a scale:

  • "She was a little annoyed" → mild
  • "She got upset" → moderate
  • "She flipped out" → strong, visible, emotional outburst
  • "She went completely berserk" → extreme

So "flip out" sits comfortably on the strong end of the scale, but it is used far more casually in everyday speech than something like "go berserk" or "have a meltdown." It doesn't necessarily mean someone did something dramatic — it just means their emotional reaction was noticeably intense.
Tone and Register — When Can You Use It?

"Flip out" is informal slang. This means:

✅ You can use it with friends, family, or in casual conversation.
✅ You can use it in informal writing, text messages, or social media.
❌ Avoid it in formal writing, business emails, academic essays, or professional settings.

Instead of "flip out" in formal contexts, you might say:

  • "She became extremely distressed."
  • "He reacted very strongly."
  • "She was overcome with excitement."

Knowing related expressions will sharpen your understanding of "flip out" by showing what it sits alongside in the language:

  • "Lose it" — Very similar. Means to lose emotional control. (He completely lost it when he heard the news.)
  • "Freak out" — Almost identical in meaning to "flip out." Very common. (She freaked out before the exam.)
  • "Blow a fuse" — Means to suddenly get very angry. (Dad blew a fuse when I came home late.)
  • "Hit the roof" — Means to get extremely angry. (My boss hit the roof when he saw the report.)
  • "Go ballistic" — Means to explode in intense anger. (She went ballistic when she found out.)
  • "Go nuts" — Can mean intense anger OR intense excitement, just like "flip out." (They went nuts when the team scored.)

Among all of these, "freak out" is the closest synonym to "flip out" — they are nearly interchangeable in most situations.

Mistake 1: Confusing it with "flip off"
"Flip off" is a completely different expression — it means to make a rude hand gesture at someone. Don't confuse the two.

Mistake 2: Using it in formal writing
Since it's slang, using "flip out" in a formal essay or professional email will sound out of place.

Mistake 3: Forgetting it can be positive
Many learners only associate "flip out" with anger. But remember — it can mean being overwhelmed with excitement, too. Always read the context.

"Flip out" means to suddenly and visibly lose control of your emotions — usually from anger, shock, panic, or extreme excitement.

If you remember that image of a switch snapping or a lid flying off a boiling pot, you will never forget what "flip out" means.
6303: The word "flip-flop" has three distinct meanings — one everyday, one social/political, and one technical. Each meaning is unrelated to the others in terms of usage, but they all share a common underlying idea, which I'll point out at the end.

The most common, everyday meaning of "flip-flop" is a simple, flat, open sandal.

It has a flat sole — the part your foot rests on — and a single strap shaped like the letter Y or V. This strap passes between your big toe and the toe next to it, anchoring the sandal to your foot. That's it. There's no back support, no laces, no buckle.

Flip-flops are extremely casual footwear. You can slip them on and off in seconds. They're popular at beaches, swimming pools, and in warm or tropical climates. Because they leave your feet largely uncovered, they are generally not considered appropriate for formal occasions, offices, or smart-casual settings in many cultures.

The name "flip-flop" is onomatopoeic — it imitates the sound the sandal makes. As you walk, the sole slaps rhythmically against your heel: flip... flop... flip... flop. That slapping sound gave the sandal its name.

You might also know these sandals by other regional names: thongs in Australia, slippers in parts of South and Southeast Asia, jandals in New Zealand, or chappal in South Asia.
Meaning 2: A sudden reversal of opinion or position

In everyday English — especially in politics, journalism, and public debate — a "flip-flop" means a sudden, complete reversal of a previously stated position, belief, or decision.

Think of a coin lying flat. It has two sides: heads and tails. Now imagine it being flipped over. That image captures the idea perfectly: a person goes from holding one position entirely to holding the opposite position.

Example: A politician campaigns on the promise "I will never raise taxes." Two years later, she supports and votes for a tax increase. People would say she "did a flip-flop" — or that her stance was a flip-flop.

The word carries a strongly negative tone. Calling something a flip-flop implies that the person is inconsistent, untrustworthy, or opportunistic — that they changed their position not out of honest reflection, but out of political pressure, personal gain, or a desire to please a different audience. It's an accusation of unreliability.

This is an important distinction: a flip-flop is not the same as a genuine change of mind. If someone says, "I used to oppose this policy, but after learning new evidence, I now support it," that is seen as intellectual honesty — it wouldn't typically be called a flip-flop. The term "flip-flop" is reserved for reversals that appear sudden, self-serving, or unexplained.

The word is most frequently used in political commentary and journalism, but it appears in everyday conversation too. For instance: "Last week you said you wanted to take a road trip. Now you want to fly. You keep flip-flopping on the plan!"

This is the most technical of the three meanings. It belongs to the world of electronics and computer science.

In digital electronics, a flip-flop is a type of circuit — and one of the most fundamentally important ones in all of computing.

First, a bit of background

Digital electronics deals entirely in two values: 0 and 1. You can think of these as "off" and "on," or "low voltage" and "high voltage." Every operation inside a computer — calculations, storing data, displaying images — ultimately comes down to processing enormous quantities of 0s and 1s.

What a flip-flop does

A flip-flop is a circuit that can exist in exactly one of two stable states at any given moment: state 0 or state 1. Once it settles into a state, it stays there — holding that value — until an external electrical signal tells it to switch. When it switches, it goes from 0 to 1 or from 1 to 0. Then it holds that new state, again indefinitely, until told to switch again.

This behavior of alternating between two stable positions is exactly why it's called a "flip-flop."

Why flip-flops matter: memory

Here is the crucial insight: because a flip-flop can hold a value of 0 or 1 — and keep holding it even after the input signal is gone — it acts as a one-bit memory cell.

It sounds simple, but this is profoundly important. A single flip-flop is the most elementary form of digital memory: it remembers one thing (a 0 or a 1). When you group multiple flip-flops together, they form what are called registers — tiny but extremely fast memory units inside a processor (CPU). Registers hold the values that the processor is actively computing with at any instant.

So every time your computer, phone, or any digital device "remembers" a value — even for a microsecond — flip-flops are involved. They are the atoms of digital memory.

Types of flip-flops

Several standard types of flip-flop circuits exist, each with slightly different rules about how and when they change state:

SR flip-flop (Set-Reset): The most basic type. It has two inputs: S (Set) and R (Reset). A signal at S forces the output to 1; a signal at R forces it to 0. One problem: if you signal S and R at the same time, the output becomes undefined and unpredictable — this is called the "forbidden state."

D flip-flop (Data or Delay): Has one data input (D) and a clock input. Each time a clock pulse arrives, the flip-flop "captures" whatever value (0 or 1) is currently present at D and holds it. This eliminates the forbidden-state problem of the SR type, making it far more practical and widely used — especially in registers.

JK flip-flop: A refined version of the SR flip-flop. It cleverly resolves the forbidden-state problem: when both inputs (J and K) are signaled at the same time, instead of behaving unpredictably, the output simply toggles — it flips to whatever state it was not in. This makes it more versatile than the SR type.

T flip-flop (Toggle): Has a single input, T. When T is 1 and a clock pulse arrives, the output flips to the opposite state (0 becomes 1, or 1 becomes 0). When T is 0, the output stays unchanged. This is the simplest toggling behavior possible, and it is especially useful in building counters — circuits that count clock pulses.

Despite their differences, all four types share the same core property: two stable states, the ability to switch between them on command, and the ability to hold the current state in between commands.

Less commonly, "flip-flop" is used informally in gymnastics and acrobatics to describe a back handspring — a move where a gymnast springs backward, plants their hands on the floor, and flips their legs over to land on their feet again. The move resembles the back-and-forth flipping motion the name suggests. This use is informal and specific to the sport, but worth knowing.
The thread connecting all three meanings

All three primary meanings of "flip-flop" share a single underlying image: switching back and forth between two opposite states.

  • The sandal makes a back-and-forth slapping motion as you walk.
  • The opinion reversal involves switching from one stance to its complete opposite.
  • The electronic circuit switches between the two binary states — 0 and 1.

This idea of a two-state toggle, of going from one extreme to the other, is the conceptual heartbeat of the word in every context it's used.
6304:
When someone flip-flops, they completely reverse their position or opinion on something — and then often reverse it again, or do so repeatedly. The word captures a very specific kind of change: one that looks inconsistent, unreliable, or driven by pressure and convenience rather than genuine understanding.

Think of a physical flip-flop sandal — it slaps forward, then slaps back. That alternating, back-and-forth motion is exactly the image the word carries into its verb form.
What makes it different from simply "changing your mind"

This is the most important distinction to understand.

Changing your mind is neutral. If someone learns new facts, studies the evidence more carefully, and revises their view as a result, that's reasonable. We might even call it growth. Nobody usually criticises a person for that.

But flip-flopping is different. It carries a negative charge. When you say someone flip-flopped, you are implying:

  • They changed their position not because of new evidence or logic, but because of external pressure — public criticism, losing votes, wanting to please a crowd, or simply because the wind changed direction.
  • Their original position was not a deeply held conviction — it was something they said for convenience or effect.
  • They cannot be trusted to stay consistent. What they say today may not be what they say tomorrow.
  • They appear spineless, opportunistic, or dishonest.

In short: changing your mind = a sign of thinking. Flip-flopping = a sign of weakness, inconsistency, or self-interest.

Flip-flopping can refer to:

  1. A single reversal — You said X, then you completely said the opposite, Y. Even one such reversal can be called a flip-flop if it looks unprincipled.
  2. Repeated back-and-forth — You said X, then Y, then back to X again. This is the fuller, more classic image of flip-flopping — swinging from one position to the other without any firm ground beneath your feet.

Both uses are common, but the repeated back-and-forth version is what the word most vividly evokes.

Flip-flop is informal. You will hear it in casual conversation, in political commentary, in news headlines, and in opinion writing. You would not typically see it in an academic paper or a formal legal document — those settings would use phrases like "reversed his position" or "altered her stance."

The word almost always carries a critical or mocking tone. When someone says "she flip-flopped on that issue," they are not being neutral — they are criticising her for it. The word is a weapon in debates and arguments, used to paint the other side as untrustworthy.
Where you will most commonly encounter it

Politics is by far the most common home for this word. Politicians are constantly watched for consistency, so any reversal gets scrutinised. Opponents love to accuse each other of flip-flopping because it makes the other person look like they stand for nothing.

But the word appears in many other areas:

  • Business and leadership — A CEO who says the company will expand, then reverses course entirely, then hints at expanding again, might be called a flip-flopper by frustrated employees or investors.
  • Personal relationships — "He keeps flip-flopping on whether he wants to be in this relationship. One week he's all in, the next week he pulls away." Here it describes emotional inconsistency.
  • Social media and public opinion — A celebrity who takes a strong public stand on an issue and then quietly walks it back, or takes the opposite position later, might be accused of flip-flopping.
  • Everyday decisions — Even in small things: "Stop flip-flopping — just pick a restaurant!" Here it's used more lightly, without the serious connotation of political dishonesty, just to mean someone cannot make up their mind and keeps going back and forth.
How to use it in a sentence (grammar)

The most natural structure is:

[Subject] + flip-flopped + on + [the issue]

"The senator flip-flopped on climate policy."
"She flip-flopped on whether to accept the job offer."
"He has been flip-flopping on this for weeks."
"The government flip-flopped under pressure from business groups."

You can use it without specifying the issue, if the topic is already understood:

"Critics accused him of flip-flopping."
"She has a reputation for flip-flopping."

The preposition "on" is the standard connector when you name the topic. You would not say "flip-flopped about" or "flip-flopped regarding" — "on" is the natural, idiomatic choice.

The continuous form — "flip-flopping" — is very common, especially to describe an ongoing pattern:

"He keeps flip-flopping."
"The administration is flip-flopping on tariffs again."
A detailed example to tie it all together

Imagine a politician named Senator Rajan. In 2022, he gives a passionate speech saying: "We must raise the minimum wage. It's a matter of basic dignity."

Then in 2023, under pressure from business lobby groups who fund his campaign, he says: "Actually, raising the minimum wage would hurt small businesses. I'm opposed to it now."

Then in 2024, with elections approaching and polls showing the public supports the wage increase, he says: "I have always believed in fair wages. We should raise the minimum wage."

A journalist watching this would write: "Senator Rajan has flip-flopped on the minimum wage multiple times, driven not by principle but by political convenience."

Notice what the journalist is saying: it's not that Rajan learned something new that changed his mind. He moved with the wind — with money and with public opinion polls. That is the essence of flip-flopping.
A lighter use to complete the picture

It is worth noting that in less serious, everyday speech, flip-flop loses some of its sharp political edge and simply means to be indecisive or to keep going back and forth:

"We've been flip-flopping between painting the walls white or beige for a month. Just pick one!"

Here, nobody is accusing anyone of being dishonest or unprincipled. It's just a casual, slightly exasperated way to say someone cannot commit to a decision. This softer use is common in friendly conversation.

To flip-flop means to reverse your position or decision — often repeatedly — in a way that looks inconsistent, unprincipled, or driven by outside pressure rather than genuine conviction. It is informal, almost always critical in tone, and most at home in political language, though it travels easily into everyday life.
6305:
Flippancy is the quality of treating something serious, sensitive, or important as though it is trivial, amusing, or not worth genuine care. It is a kind of careless lightness — a breezy, dismissive attitude applied to something that truly deserves respect, thought, or gravity.

When someone displays flippancy, they are essentially saying, "I don't think this is worth taking seriously," — often without saying those words directly. They say it through their tone, their jokes, or their casual remarks.

Think of it this way: every situation has a kind of emotional weight — a level of seriousness it deserves. A funeral is heavy. A crisis is urgent. A person sharing their deepest pain is vulnerable.

Flippancy is when someone refuses to match that weight. Instead of rising to meet the seriousness of the moment, they deliberately — or carelessly — stay light, breezy, and dismissive. They crack a joke when silence was needed. They shrug off something that deserved a thoughtful response. They make a careless comment when careful words were called for.
What It Looks Like in Real Life

Imagine a student fails an important exam and is genuinely distressed. They tell a friend about it, clearly upset. The friend responds with, "Oh well, exams are just numbers anyway! Who cares?"

That response is flippancy. The friend didn't engage with the real pain. They brushed past it with a dismissive, carefree remark — not because they were being comforting, but because they weren't taking the situation seriously at all.

Another example: A journalist interviews a politician about a serious public health crisis. The politician responds with jokes and cheerful slogans, avoiding the gravity of the issue entirely. That is flippancy in a public, professional context.

For something to qualify as flippancy, it usually contains these elements:

1. A serious subject is involved.
Flippancy only really lands as flippancy when the topic genuinely deserves seriousness. You can't be flippant about something already trivial — the contrast is what makes it noticeable.

2. The response is inappropriately light.
The person responds with casual language, humor, sarcasm, breezy dismissal, or an airy attitude that does not match the gravity of what is being discussed.

3. There is a sense of disrespect — intentional or not.
Flippancy disrespects either the subject, the person raising it, or both. Even if the flippant person doesn't mean to be offensive, their carelessness communicates a lack of regard.

Not necessarily, and this is an important nuance.

Sometimes flippancy is deliberate — a person uses it as a defence mechanism to avoid uncomfortable emotions. If something feels too painful or too heavy, some people instinctively deflect with humour or casualness, shielding themselves from having to engage emotionally. This is flippancy used as armour.

Other times, flippancy is unconscious — a person simply doesn't realize how serious the situation is, and their natural lightness comes across as dismissive and disrespectful, even though they didn't mean harm.

And sometimes, flippancy is intentional and cutting — used to belittle something or someone, to signal that the speaker considers the topic beneath them.

In all three cases, the result is the same: a mismatch between the seriousness the situation deserved and the lightness that was offered instead.

This is where many learners get confused, so let's be precise.

Flippancy is not the same as humour.
Humour, when used well and at the right moment, can be deeply appropriate — even comforting. A well-timed, gentle joke can ease tension, bring people together, and acknowledge pain without dismissing it. Flippancy, by contrast, dismisses. The difference lies in whether the lightness serves the moment or disrespects it.

Flippancy is not the same as being casual or relaxed.
You can have a relaxed, easygoing conversation about something serious and still be fully respectful and engaged. Flippancy is not about your style of speaking — it's about your underlying attitude of dismissal.

Flippancy is not the same as sarcasm.
Sarcasm means saying one thing while meaning another, usually to mock or criticize. You can be sarcastic while still being deeply serious about a topic. Flippancy is specifically about a lack of seriousness, not about a verbal technique.

Flippancy is not the same as being brief.
A short, direct answer is not flippant. Flippancy is in the dismissive spirit of a response, not its length.
The Feeling It Creates in Others

When someone is on the receiving end of flippancy, it tends to feel like being waved away — like your concern, your pain, or the topic you raised just wasn't worth the other person's genuine attention. It can feel belittling, frustrating, or even hurtful, especially when you were vulnerable or earnest about something.

This is why flippancy is generally considered a negative quality. It signals either emotional immaturity, a lack of empathy, or a deliberate air of superiority over the subject at hand.

• "His flippancy during the serious meeting left everyone feeling that he didn't care about the issue at all."
  • "She responded to her brother's worries with a flippancy that stung him deeply."
  • "The interviewer was irritated by the candidate's flippancy when asked about his previous failures."
  • "There was a time for laughter and a time for gravity — his flippancy showed he couldn't tell the difference."

Flippancy is the quality of being carelessly or disrespectfully light-hearted about something that genuinely deserves to be taken seriously.

It is not wrong to be cheerful. It is not wrong to have a sense of humour. It becomes flippancy the moment that lightness is applied where gravity was needed — dismissing what deserved to be honoured.
6306:
When someone is flippant, they treat a serious or important matter as if it is trivial — with a casual, breezy attitude that clearly does not belong in the situation. A flippant person essentially sends this message: "I don't find this important enough to take seriously." That signal, whether they mean to send it or not, is what makes flippancy so frustrating and often rude to others.

The single most important thing to understand about this word is that it describes a mismatch — a mismatch between how serious a situation is and how lightly a person responds to it.
What it looks like in real life

Imagine a student who failed an important exam. They go to their teacher and say, "I worked really hard for this. I don't understand what went wrong." And the teacher shrugs and says, "Well, can't win 'em all!" and walks away smiling. That teacher is being flippant. The student's concern was real and deserved a thoughtful response, but the teacher brushed it off with a light, almost jokey remark.

Or imagine someone tells a friend, "I've been feeling really depressed lately." And the friend laughs lightly and says, "Oh, everyone gets sad sometimes. Just cheer up!" That response is flippant. It dismisses something serious with a casual wave of the hand.

Or think of a politician asked a tough, important question in an interview, and instead of answering it honestly, they crack a joke and change the subject. Journalists often describe that as a flippant response.

Notice something in all three examples: the flippant person isn't necessarily being viciously cruel or aggressively rude. They're being dismissive — treating something weighty as if it weighs nothing. That casual dismissiveness is the heart of flippancy.

Flippancy often carries a tone of cleverness-without-care. A flippant person might say something witty or amusing, but at completely the wrong moment. The problem isn't the wit — it's the timing and the implied message that the serious matter at hand simply isn't worth a serious response.

Sometimes people are flippant intentionally, to avoid a difficult conversation or to appear cool and unbothered. Other times they're flippant without realizing it — they simply don't read the room and don't understand how grave the situation feels to others. Either way, the effect on others is the same: they feel dismissed, disrespected, or belittled.
How it feels to be on the receiving end

When someone is flippant toward you about something you care about, it stings in a specific way. It's not the sting of a harsh insult. It's more like the sting of being ignored or made to feel foolish for caring so much. It can make you feel that your concern was silly, that the other person thinks they're above taking it seriously, or that they simply don't respect you enough to engage honestly. This is why calling someone's remark flippant is a pointed criticism — you're saying they failed to meet the moment with the seriousness it deserved.

It's important to separate flippant from a few things it might seem similar to.

Being funny or playful is not flippant on its own. If two friends are joking around together about lighthearted things, that's just humor. Flippancy only enters the picture when lightness is used in a context that calls for seriousness.

Being flippant is also not the same as being openly rude or aggressive. Someone who shouts or insults you is being hostile. A flippant person is being dismissive — which is a quieter, more casual form of disrespect. In some ways, flippancy can sting more, because it suggests you aren't even worth a serious argument.

And flippancy is not the same as simply being brief. A person can give a short answer that is still thoughtful and respectful. A flippant answer is one that is casual and dismissive in tone and content, not just in length.
Similar words, and how flippant differs from them

Glib is perhaps the closest sibling to flippant. A glib person speaks smoothly and confidently but without real depth or sincerity. Flippant and glib often overlap, but glib focuses more on the effortless, shallow fluency of what's being said, while flippant focuses more on the disrespectful lightness with which something serious is being treated.

Frivolous means treating things as unimportant or spending time and energy on trivial things. A person can be frivolous in their general lifestyle (caring too much about unimportant things). Flippant is more specifically about a response or attitude in a particular moment.

Cavalier means showing a careless lack of concern, often in a self-assured, superior way. It's very close to flippant. The slight difference is that cavalier often implies a feeling of superiority — as if the person thinks they are above the matter — while flippant leans more into the casual, breezy, joke-making quality of the dismissal.

Facetious means joking or trying to be funny in a situation that doesn't call for it. It's very close to flippant, but facetious is specifically about attempting humor, while flippant is a broader attitude that may or may not involve jokes.

The opposite of flippant would be earnest, sincere, grave, or solemn — all words that describe taking something seriously and responding to it with the weight it deserves.
How the word is used in sentences

You'll most often see flippant paired with words like remark, comment, response, attitude, answer, tone, or reply. Here are some natural examples:

"His flippant remark about her job loss made her want to leave the room."

"She gave a flippant answer to a question that deserved real thought."

"The committee was frustrated by the manager's flippant attitude toward the safety complaints."

"Don't be so flippant — this is a serious situation."

You can also use the related noun form, flippancy, to describe the quality or behavior itself: "His flippancy during the meeting showed that he didn't respect the gravity of the issue."

Flippant means treating something serious with unearned lightness — being breezy, casual, or joke-y when the situation demands care, respect, and genuine engagement. It is a form of disrespect, even when it doesn't look as harsh as open rudeness. When you call someone flippant, you are saying: this person failed to give a serious thing the seriousness it deserved.
6307:
When you flirt with someone, you behave toward them in a way that hints you find them attractive — but you do it lightly, playfully, and without full seriousness. It's like sending a signal of romantic or sexual interest without actually declaring it openly.

Think of it as a game of gentle suggestion. You're not confessing love. You're not asking someone out directly. You're simply letting someone feel that you find them appealing — through your words, your looks, your body language, and your energy — while keeping things fun and low-stakes.

Flirting is not one single action. It's a style of behaviour made up of many small things:

  • Teasing someone gently — making a playful joke at their expense, or lightly challenging something they said, in a way that's warm rather than mean
  • Holding eye contact a moment longer than normal
  • Paying compliments that go slightly beyond what you'd say to a friend ("You look amazing in that colour")
  • Light physical touch — brushing someone's arm, leaning in close when talking
  • Being extra attentive — laughing easily at their jokes, asking them questions, making them feel like they have your full focus
  • Teasing or being mysterious — saying something that could mean two things, letting the other person wonder what you meant

None of these things alone necessarily means someone is flirting. It's the combination — the pattern of behaviour, the tone, the small signals together — that makes something flirtatious.
The Most Important Quality: It Is Playful and Non-Committal

This is what separates flirting from simply expressing romantic interest directly.

When you flirt, you are not making a serious move. There is a lightness to it. If the other person doesn't respond with interest, both people can pretend it was "nothing serious" — because technically, it wasn't. Flirting lives in a deliberately ambiguous space. It can be denied, laughed off, or escalated further, depending on how the other person responds.

This is why flirting often involves humour, teasing, and a light-hearted tone. The playfulness acts as a kind of protection. It lets you show interest without the vulnerability of a direct, honest declaration.
Flirting Can Be Mutual or One-Sided

When two people flirt with each other, they are both sending and receiving these small signals, enjoying the playful back-and-forth. This is often called "flirting with each other" or simply "flirting."

But flirting can also be one-sided — one person flirts at another who may not respond the same way, or may not even notice.

You can also flirt without any real intention. Some people flirt naturally and habitually — not because they want a relationship, but because it's simply how they interact warmly and energetically with people they like. This is sometimes called "harmless flirting" or "innocent flirting."

It helps to know what flirting is not, so the edges of the word are sharp:

  • Flirting ≠ Seducing. Seduction is more deliberate, more serious, and aimed at a clear outcome. Flirting is lighter and less goal-driven.
  • Flirting ≠ Confessing feelings. Flirting suggests feelings without stating them. "I like you" is not flirting — it's a direct statement.
  • Flirting ≠ Chatting warmly. Friendliness is not flirting, though flirting often uses friendliness as its surface. The key difference is the romantic or sexual undercurrent.
  • Flirting ≠ Harassment. Flirting is welcome or at least neutral. When someone is clearly uncomfortable and you persist, it is no longer flirting.

"Flirt" is also used figuratively — outside of romantic situations — and it carries the same idea of casual, playful, non-serious engagement with something, without fully committing to it.

"To flirt with an idea" means to think about an idea casually and with some interest, but without seriously committing to it.

"She flirted with the idea of moving to another country, but never actually did anything about it."

"To flirt with danger / disaster / death" means to come close to something dangerous or harmful in a reckless or careless way — as if you're treating it too lightly.

"He drove at 180 km/h on a wet road, flirting with disaster."

"The company was flirting with bankruptcy for two years before it finally collapsed."

In these figurative uses, the word keeps its core flavour: being near something, engaging with it lightly, without full seriousness or full commitment.

• "She kept catching his eye across the room and smiling — she was clearly flirting with him."
  • "He flirted with her all evening, complimenting her and finding excuses to make her laugh."
  • "They had been flirting for weeks before he finally asked her out."
  • "She didn't mean anything by it — she just naturally flirts with everyone she meets."
  • "Stop flirting with the waiter and let's order our food."

To flirt is to show romantic or sexual interest in someone through playful, teasing, and suggestive behaviour — while keeping things light, non-serious, and deniable. It lives in the space between pure friendliness and open romantic pursuit. Figuratively, it also means to casually engage with an idea or situation without fully committing to it.
6308:
To flit means to move quickly and lightly from one place to another — and then move on again, without staying anywhere for long.

The key is that it is not just one quick movement. It is a series of quick, light movements, jumping from point to point, never settling. Think of a butterfly in a garden. It lands on a flower for a second, then dashes to another flower, then another. It is always moving, always brief, always light. That is flitting.

To truly understand this word, hold these three qualities together in your mind at the same time:

  1. Quick — the movement is fast, not slow or leisurely.
  2. Light — the movement has an almost effortless, airy quality to it. There is no heaviness, no force, no stomping.
  3. Brief at each stop — whatever is flitting does not settle or stay. It touches a place and moves on almost immediately.

Remove any one of these qualities and you no longer have flitting. A snail moving from leaf to leaf is quick? No — so it cannot flit. A boulder rolling down a hill is fast? Yes — but it has no lightness, no delicacy, so it cannot flit. A bird sitting on a branch for an hour? It stayed too long — not flitting.

Imagine a dragonfly hovering over a pond. It zips to one spot, hovers for a moment, zips to another, then another. Its path is not a straight line — it is irregular, darting, unpredictable. That erratic but effortless quality is very much what "flit" captures.

Or imagine a child at a birthday party running from the cake table to the balloon station to the gift pile to a friend — touching each briefly, moving on excitedly, never sitting still. That child is flitting around the room.

1. "The hummingbird flitted from flower to flower."
This is the most classic, natural use. The bird moves fast, touches briefly, moves on. Light, quick, transient.

2. "She flitted around the party, chatting with everyone for a few minutes before moving on."
Here a person is flitting socially — not committing to any one group or conversation, breezing through lightly.

3. "A shadow flitted across the wall."
The shadow appeared briefly and moved across quickly, then was gone. This shows that "flit" can describe things passing through your field of vision quickly, not just things physically jumping between locations.

4. "His eyes flitted nervously around the room."
His gaze moved rapidly from one spot to another without resting anywhere. This is "flit" applied to where attention is directed.

5. "A smile flitted across her face."
The smile appeared for just a moment and disappeared. Brief, light, gone. This is a very common figurative use.

6. "Thoughts flitted through his mind as he tried to sleep."
Different thoughts came and went quickly, none staying long enough for him to hold onto. This is "flit" applied to mental activity.

"Flit" is used very naturally in figurative language — meaning it often describes things that are not literally moving through space. The logic is always the same: something appears briefly, then passes on. These figurative uses are extremely common and important to know:

  • Expressions on a face — a smile, a frown, a look of surprise can flit across someone's face, meaning it appeared and vanished in an instant.
  • Thoughts or ideas — a thought can flit through your mind, meaning it briefly entered your consciousness but you couldn't hold onto it.
  • Attention or interest — someone's attention can flit from one thing to another, meaning they cannot focus on any one thing for long.
  • Light and shadow — a ray of light or a shadow can flit across a surface as it moves quickly over it.

When "flit" is used to describe things in nature — birds, butterflies, light, shadows — it is neutral to beautiful. It paints a graceful, lively picture.

When used to describe a person's behavior, it can carry a mild negative tone depending on context. Saying someone "flits from job to job" or "flits from relationship to relationship" suggests they are unable to commit, restless, or unwilling to put down roots. It implies a lack of depth or seriousness. Saying someone "flitted around the party" is more neutral — it just describes their social movement.

So be aware: the word itself is not negative, but when applied to human choices and commitments, it can quietly suggest unreliability or fickleness.

These are words people often confuse with "flit":

  • Dart — darting is fast and direct, usually in one sudden movement in one direction ("she darted across the street"). Flitting is repeated, irregular, and lighter.
  • Rush — rushing is fast but implies urgency and effort. Flitting is effortless and airy.
  • Wander — wandering is slow and aimless. Flitting is fast.
  • Flutter — fluttering describes a trembling or vibrating kind of movement (like wings beating rapidly, or a flag in the wind). Flitting is about the path of movement, not the physical motion of the thing itself.
  • Hover — hovering means staying in one place in the air. Flitting means moving between places. A hummingbird hovers at a flower; it flits between flowers.

In real-world usage, you will most commonly see these things described as flitting:

  • Birds, butterflies, insects, bats
  • A person's eyes or gaze
  • Thoughts or memories
  • Expressions on a face (smiles, shadows of emotion)
  • Light, shadows, reflections
  • People at social events
  • Attention or interest

If you ever need to recall this word in a flash, remember this:

To flit is to move quickly and lightly from place to place, touching briefly and moving on, never staying.

Everything else — the figurative uses, the connotations, the comparisons — flows naturally from that single core idea.
6309: To flitter means to move rapidly in a light, restless, back-and-forth or darting way — like something that can't quite stay still. Think of a candle flame in a breeze, or a butterfly that keeps zipping from flower to flower. That constant, quick, light movement — with no real settled destination — is the heart of what "flitter" means.

Sense 1: To flutter or flicker — moving rapidly back and forth

This is the most precise, dictionary-core sense. To flitter means to move back and forth very rapidly — the way a candle flitters. The movement is light and trembling, not heavy or forceful. A flame flitters. A leaf in the wind flitters. Wings flitter.

Sense 2: To move about quickly and nimbly from place to place

This is the broader, more common sense you'll encounter in everyday writing. To flitter means to move about rapidly and nimbly, or to move quickly from one condition or location to another. Here the emphasis is less on back-and-forth trembling and more on quick, light, restless movement across a space. Think of birds flittering back and forth between a backyard feeder and the safety of the trees.

Both senses share the same soul: light, quick, restless movement.

This is an important subtlety. "Flitter" is built from the word flit, but it carries something extra. It implies the action happening repeatedly, continuously — not just once. If something flitters, it isn't making one quick dart and stopping. It keeps going — back and forth, here and there, over and over. This is what gives the word its sense of restlessness and busyness.

When used literally, flitter describes the physical movement of real objects:

  • A butterfly flittering among flowers.
  • A bat flittering silently around a garden at dusk.
  • A flame flittering in the wind.
  • A flock of pigeons caused to flap and flitter around.
  • Monarch butterflies flittering and fluttering on a hike.

Notice the things that flitter are almost always small, light, and airborne — or at least delicate. Heavy things don't flitter. A truck doesn't flitter. A boulder doesn't flitter. The word carries an inherent sense of lightness.

"Flitter" is also beautifully used for things that aren't physical — ideas, feelings, time, particles. Anything that seems to dart about in a light, fleeting, hard-to-pin-down way can "flitter."

  • A writer's neuroses can flitter around him like fireflies.
  • Subatomic particles can flitter across the screen in a film.
  • A pocket of time can flitter away before you know it — gone almost as soon as it arrived.

In the figurative sense, "flitter" often carries a slight feeling of elusiveness — the thing is there, but it won't hold still, and you can't quite grasp it.
How It Compares to Similar Words

These words are all close cousins, and it helps to see how they differ:

Flit — a single, quick, light movement from one point to another. Sharp and sudden. One action. "The bird flitted to the branch."

Flitter — like flit, but repeated and continuous. The action keeps happening. "The bird flittered about the garden" — it kept darting here and there.

Flutter — more about the rapid, trembling movement in place or with wings/edges. A heart flutters (trembles). A flag flutters (waves rapidly). Flitter and flutter overlap a lot, and are often used interchangeably, but flutter tends to feel more about the trembling motion itself, while flitter tends to feel more about moving from place to place.

Flicker — mostly about light or something visual that rapidly shifts between visible and not — a flame flickers, a light flickers. Flitter can overlap with this too, but flicker is more specifically about the on-off quality of light or visibility.
The Overall Feel of the Word

"Flitter" is a word that feels exactly like what it describes — light, quick, and a little delicate. When you read or hear it, picture something small, airy, and in constant, restless motion — never settled, always moving, always just out of reach. Whether it's a butterfly above a meadow, a bat in the evening air, a thought darting through the mind, or a moment of time vanishing before you can catch it — that is what it means to flitter.
